notes.b: A nuclear family is a parent or parents with their dependent children, living together in a self-contained household.
points: Two parents, married or cohabiting, and their dependent children form one self-contained household.
The unit is small and mobile, so members can move for work, which often separates the family from relatives.
Tasks, child rearing and decision-making are usually shared between both parents.
Children depend mainly on the parents' income and on State supports such as Child Benefit.
A lone-parent family is one parent living with one or more dependent children.
Causes include separation, divorce, the death of a partner, and a parent's choice to raise a child alone.
The lone parent carries the full economic, emotional and workload responsibility, often on one income.
Lone parents who work need reliable childcare, and may depend on relatives or on the One-Parent Family Payment.
Lone parenthood can be temporary, ending when the children grow up or when a new partner joins the household.

notes.b: An extended family includes wider relatives beyond the parents and children, and its members stay closely linked.
points: Members include grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, who live in the same household or close by.
Members are interdependent, sharing childcare, housework, money and care for older relatives.
Members often work together as one economic unit, such as a family farm or family business.
Historically, roles were segregated by gender, with men and women carrying out separate tasks.
Extended families are common in many cultures, where grandparents often provide much of the childcare.

notes.b: A blended family forms when one or both partners bring children from an earlier relationship into a new union.
points: Blended families arise through remarriage or cohabitation, and sometimes after the death of a spouse.
Step-parents, step-siblings and half-siblings may all live in the household, creating new relationships.
The adults must agree on rules and discipline, which can be difficult when children have different expectations.
Parents may have financial obligations to children from an earlier relationship as well as to children of the new union.
A joint child of the new partners creates a sibling group that differs in age and background from the earlier children.

notes.h: Comparing Irish families with European families (settings)
points: Structure: compare the proportions of nuclear, lone-parent, extended and blended households, using the most recent published statistics.
Size: compare the number of children per family and how family size has changed since the mid-twentieth century.
Roles: Nordic countries provide State-funded parental leave and childcare, which supports shared parenting.
Roles: in many southern European countries grandparents often provide much of the childcare, and adult children may remain at home longer.
State support: compare how far each country relies on the State and on the extended family to support parents.

questions.prompt: Identify and describe two modern family structures.
questions.model: Two structures, each identified and described. Lone-parent family: one parent living with one or more dependent children, arising through separation, bereavement or choice. Blended family: partners with children from earlier relationships, arising through remarriage or cohabitation, with step-relationships and rules to agree. Accept any two of nuclear, extended, lone-parent or blended, with accurate descriptions.

questions.prompt: Compare the characteristics of lone-parent families and extended families, and explain the challenges each type of family may face.
questions.model: Lone-parent family: one parent and dependent children; one income; full economic, emotional and workload responsibility; reliance on childcare and on relatives or State supports such as the One-Parent Family Payment. Challenges include financial pressure, role overload and limited time. Extended family: parents, children and wider relatives living together or nearby; interdependence; shared childcare, housework and money; often one economic unit. Challenges include segregated roles, dependence on the older generation, and conflict over authority and living space. Comparison: the lone-parent family has one adult to share responsibilities, while the extended family has several adults but may have shared expectations to manage.
